title: Coordinate Geometry
description: Class 9 IMO — Coordinate Geometry: the Cartesian plane and its quadrants, plotting points, abscissa and ordinate, points on the axes, and distance using Pythagoras.

topics.title: The Cartesian Plane
topics.concept:
What is the Cartesian Plane?

The Cartesian plane (or coordinate plane) is a two-dimensional plane formed by two perpendicular number lines: the x-axis (horizontal) and the y-axis (vertical). Their intersection point is called the origin, denoted by O(0, 0).

What are Coordinates of a Point?

A point's coordinates are an ordered pair (x, y) that tells its exact location on the plane:

  • The x-coordinate (abscissa) tells how far to move left or right from the origin
  • The y-coordinate (ordinate) tells how far to move up or down from the origin

How to Plot a Point (x, y):

  1. Start at the origin (0, 0)
  2. Move horizontally: x units right (if x > 0) or left (if x < 0)
  3. Move vertically: y units up (if y > 0) or down (if y < 0)
  4. Mark the point where you end

Real-Life Applications:

  • Maps and GPS navigation (latitude and longitude)
  • Video game character positioning
  • Architectural blueprints and floor plans
  • Air traffic control radar screens

Its x-coordinate is 0, so it lies on the y-axis (no quadrant).

recap: Axes meet at the origin (0, 0); quadrants are numbered anticlockwise.
Signs (±, ±) fix the quadrant; points on an axis are in none.

quiz.q: Find the distance between P(−3, 2) and Q(5, 2).
quiz.explanation: Same y-coordinate, so the distance is |5 − (−3)| = 8 units.

quiz.q: If A(x, 4) lies on a line parallel to the y-axis passing through B(5, −2), then x is:
quiz.explanation: A line parallel to the y-axis has a constant x; through B(5, −2) it is x = 5, so x = 5.

topics.title: Plotting Points: Abscissa and Ordinate
topics.concept:
How to Plot Points Systematically:

Plotting means marking a point on the Cartesian plane given its coordinates (x, y).

Step-by-Step Plotting Process:

  1. Locate the origin (0, 0)
  2. Move horizontally along the x-axis to the x-coordinate
  3. From that position, move vertically to the y-coordinate
  4. Mark and label the point

Plotting Points with Same x or Same y:

  • Points with same x-coordinate lie on a vertical line
  • Points with same y-coordinate lie on a horizontal line

Plotting Multiple Points:

When plotting several points, it helps to:

  • Plot all points first
  • Label each point clearly
  • Identify patterns (collinear points, shapes)

Connecting Points:

Points can be connected to form geometric shapes:

  • Triangles (3 points)
  • Rectangles and squares (4 points)
  • Other polygons

examples.solution: No — coordinates are ordered, so they are different points.

recap: Order matters: (x, y) ≠ (y, x) in general.

quiz.q: The base BC of a triangle lies along the x-axis with the origin as its midpoint. If B is (−3, 0), then C is:
quiz.explanation: If the origin is the midpoint and B is 3 units left at (−3, 0), then C is 3 units right at (3, 0).

quiz.q: A point P is 4 units from the x-axis and 3 units from the y-axis, in Quadrant III. Its coordinates are:
quiz.explanation: |y| = 4 and |x| = 3; in Quadrant III both are negative, so (−3, −4).

topics.title: Distance Between Points (Pythagoras)
topics.concept:
For points sharing a coordinate, the distance is just the difference of the other coordinate. For a general pair, drop a right triangle: the horizontal leg is the difference in x, the vertical leg the difference in y, and the distance is the hypotenuse by Pythagoras.

So the gap between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].

examples.solution: Same y, so it is just 4 − 1 = 3 units.

recap: Same-row/column points: subtract the differing coordinate.

quiz.q: Rohan sits at (3, 4). He is moved to a seat with the same abscissa but with the ordinate reduced by 5. His new position is:
quiz.explanation: Abscissa stays 3 and ordinate becomes 4 − 5 = −1, giving (3, −1).

quiz.q: Station Alpha is at (−4, 2) and Station Beta at (6, 2). A hub lies exactly halfway between them at:
quiz.explanation: Midpoint x = (−4 + 6)/2 = 1, y = 2, so the hub is (1, 2).

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: (0, 3) has x = 0 so it lies on the y-axis, and R correctly explains this.

questions.q: If (a, b) lies in Quadrant II, then (−a, −b) lies in:
questions.explanation: In Quadrant II, a < 0 and b > 0, so −a > 0 and −b < 0, which is Quadrant IV.

questions.q: A point has equal non-zero numerical values for its abscissa and ordinate (|x| = |y|). On which line can it NOT lie?
questions.explanation: |x| = |y| means y = x or y = −x (i.e. x + y = 0). The line x + y = 5 need not satisfy |x| = |y|.
